newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, facing heart surgery, to meet Kohl.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, facing heart surgery, to meet Kohl.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, preparing to undergo heart surgery, meets German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday after being urged by his own security chief to hand over power until he regains his health.
Yeltsin, whose announcement he would have the operation ended months of equivocation over the state of his health, was due to meet Kohl, a personal friend, at the Rus husting lodge outside Moscow.
It will be his first encounter with a Western head of government since he was elected on July 3 to a second four-year term in the Kremlin. He has rarely been seen in public since late June.

A German government spokesman said the schedule for the meeting had not been changed despite Yeltsin's forthcoming operation. German officials have said Kohl's visit is an informal affair with no urgent agenda.
A surgeon told Interfax news agency Yeltsin would undergo a relatively routine bypass operation to relieve the ischaemia which put the 65-year-old leader in hospital twice last year.
But national security chief Alexander Lebed said the time had come for Yeltsin to name Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to govern the country until he recovered his health.

"A situation has arisen where someone (Yeltsin) is temporarily unable to carry out his duties. For that period, by his order or decree, a person who would run the country and be responsible for what is going on should be clearly defined and named -- and his name is Chernomyrdin," Lebed said.
Under the constitution, if the president is unable to carry out his duties, the prime minister stands in for him for up to three months, after which new elections must be held.

Yeltsin's prolonged absence from the political centre stage sparked speculation about a power vacuum in the Kremlin and a struggle for influence between Lebed, Chernomyrdin and presidential chief of staff Anatoly Chubais.
Lebed discussed the issue in talks with Chubais which also covered the peace plan which he reached last week with separatist rebels in the southern region of Chechnya.

Yeltsin has given his partial backing to the plan to end 21 months of fighting. It provides for the withdrawal of most Russian troops but puts off a decision on the political status of the mainly Moslem southern region for five years.

Lebed, speaking as thousands of Chechens across the region celebrated the fifth anniversary of their declaration of independence, said on the commercial NTV channel that the troop withdrawal would begin on Sunday.
Separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who attended a celebration in the village of Tsotsin-Yurt, told Russian Television that Yeltsin's health would not affect the peace process.
Valery Sadrikov, deputy head of the Surgical Centre of the Academy of Medical Sciences, said Yeltsin would have the bypass at Moscow's Cardiological Centre, headed by Yevgeny Chazov.
Millions of heart bypass operations have been carried out around the world since the 1960s. Most patients have been able to return to work within about a month.
